learn.hook: Long before anyone knew about DNA, a monk counted thousands of pea plants and cracked the code of heredity with simple arithmetic.
points: Inheritance is the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny; it is the basis of heredity. Variation is the degree by which progeny differ from their parents. Genetics is the branch of biology dealing with inheritance and variation.

Humans knew from as early as 8000–1000 B.C. that one cause of variation was hidden in sexual reproduction. They used natural variation in wild populations for selective breeding and artificial selection, e.g. the Sahiwal cows of Punjab.

Gregor Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas for seven years (1856–1863) and proposed the laws of inheritance. He was the first to apply statistical analysis and mathematical logic to biology, and his large sample sizes gave credibility to his data.

He used true-breeding lines: plants that, through continuous self-pollination, show stable trait inheritance over several generations. He selected 14 true-breeding varieties as 7 pairs differing in one character with contrasting traits.

The seven pairs (dominant first): stem height tall/dwarf; flower colour violet/white; flower position axial/terminal; pod shape inflated/constricted; pod colour green/yellow; seed shape round/wrinkled; seed colour yellow/green.

example.q: How many true-breeding pea varieties did Mendel select for his seven characters, and why were large samples important?
steps: 7 characters × 2 contrasting traits each = 14 true-breeding varieties.
Large samples reduce chance effects, so the ratios he saw were reliable.
example.answer: 14 varieties; large samples made his statistical conclusions credible.

learn.reallife: Sahiwal and Gir cattle, prized by Indian dairy farmers for heat tolerance and milk yield, are products of centuries of artificial selection based on natural variation.

topics.title: Monohybrid cross, Punnett square and test cross

learn.hook: Two tall pea plants can produce a dwarf one. The dwarf trait was hiding in plain sight, and the Punnett square shows exactly where.
points: Mendel crossed true-breeding tall and dwarf plants. The F1 (first filial) generation was all tall. On self-pollination of F1, the F2 showed tall : dwarf in a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio; the dwarf trait reappeared unchanged.

He proposed 'factors' (now called genes) that pass unchanged from parent to offspring. Genes coding for a pair of contrasting traits are alleles. In TT and tt both alleles are the same (homozygous); in Tt they differ (heterozygous). Genotype is the genetic make-up (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is the observable trait (tall, dwarf). Tall (T) is the dominant trait; dwarf (t) is recessive.
The Punnett square, developed by the British geneticist Reginald C. Punnett, shows all possible gamete combinations. For Tt × Tt: genotypes TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1; phenotypes tall : dwarf = 3 : 1.

Test cross: an organism with the dominant phenotype is crossed with the recessive parent (tt) to find its genotype. If all progeny are dominant, it is TT; if half dominant and half recessive (1 : 1), it is Tt.

example.q: A tall pea plant crossed with a dwarf plant gives 48 tall and 46 dwarf progeny. What is the genotype of the tall plant?
steps: This is a test cross (crossed with recessive tt).
Progeny ratio is about 1 : 1 tall : dwarf.
A 1 : 1 ratio arises only if the tall parent is heterozygous Tt.

learn.reallife: Seed companies in Hyderabad run test crosses to confirm that parent lines are pure before producing hybrid seed, exactly this logic.

teach.nudge: Good! What cross reveals the genotype of a tall plant, and what ratio would a Tt plant give?

topics.title: Laws of dominance and segregation; incomplete dominance

learn.hook: Cross a red snapdragon with a white one and you get neither red nor white, but pink. Mendel's dominance rule has exceptions.
points: Law of dominance: (i) characters are controlled by discrete units called factors; (ii) factors occur in pairs; (iii) in a dissimilar pair, one member (dominant) dominates the other (recessive). It explains the uniform F1 and the 3 : 1 F2.

Law of segregation: alleles do not show any blending; both characters are recovered as such in F2. The two alleles of a pair segregate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one of the two factors. A homozygous parent produces one kind of gamete; a heterozygous parent produces two kinds in equal proportion.

Incomplete dominance: the F1 has a phenotype intermediate between the parents. In dog flower (snapdragon, Antirrhinum sp.), red (RR) × white (rr) gives pink (Rr) F1. F2 gives red : pink : white = 1 : 2 : 1, the same as the genotypic ratio.

Understanding dominance through gene products: a gene carries information for a product, often an enzyme. A modified allele may produce a normal enzyme (equivalent to the original), a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme. The unmodified allele that produces a functional product usually acts dominant; the modified one that gives a non-functional or less efficient product is usually recessive.

example.q: In snapdragon, a pink-flowered plant is self-pollinated, giving 160 plants. How many red, pink and white plants are expected?
steps: Rr × Rr gives RR : Rr : rr = 1 : 2 : 1.
With incomplete dominance, phenotypes are red : pink : white = 1 : 2 : 1.

learn.reallife: Florists in Pune who grow snapdragons and similar ornamentals use such crosses to predict flower colour mixes for festival orders.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What do the laws of dominance and segregation say, and why are some snapdragons pink?'
teach.praise: Brilliant! One allele dominates, alleles separate into gametes, and in snapdragon incomplete dominance gives pink with a 1 : 2 : 1 F2.
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to alleles during gamete formation, and what is the F2 ratio in snapdragon?

topics.title: Co-dominance, multiple alleles and blood-group crosses

learn.hook: Your blood group AB proves that two alleles can be fully expressed together, with neither hiding the other.
points: Co-dominance: the F1 resembles both parents. The ABO blood groups are controlled by gene I with three alleles, Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i. Iᴬ and Iᴮ produce slightly different forms of a sugar on the RBC surface; i produces no sugar.
Iᴬ and Iᴮ are completely dominant over i. When Iᴬ and Iᴮ are together, both express their sugars: blood group AB. This is co-dominance.

Multiple allelism: more than two alleles govern the same character. It is seen only when population studies are made, since an individual has only two alleles. With three alleles there are six genotypes and four phenotypes: IᴬIᴬ, Iᴬi (A); IᴮIᴮ, Iᴮi (B); IᴬIᴮ (AB); ii (O).

Dominance depends on the trait studied: in pea, gene B controls starch synthesis. BB seeds have large starch grains and are round; bb seeds have small grains and are wrinkled; Bb seeds are round but have intermediate-sized grains. So for seed shape B is dominant, but for starch grain size it shows incomplete dominance.

example.q: A man of blood group A (Iᴬi) marries a woman of blood group B (Iᴮi). What blood groups can their children have and in what ratio?
steps: Gametes: man Iᴬ or i; woman Iᴮ or i.
Combinations: IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴬi (A), Iᴮi (B), ii (O), each 1/4.

learn.reallife: Blood banks in Indian hospitals cross-match ABO groups before transfusion, because the RBC surface sugars coded by these alleles trigger immune reactions if mismatched.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why is my blood group AB, and how many ABO genotypes are there?'
teach.praise: Excellent! Iᴬ and Iᴮ are co-dominant, giving AB; three alleles give six genotypes and four phenotypes.
teach.nudge: Good! What do we call it when both alleles are expressed, and how many genotypes are there?

learn.hook: Sixteen boxes in a Punnett square hold the most famous ratio in biology: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
points: Mendel crossed round yellow (RRYY) with wrinkled green (rryy). F1 was all round yellow (RrYy). F1 selfed gave F2 round yellow : round green : wrinkled yellow : wrinkled green = 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Each character still segregates 3 : 1 independently: round : wrinkled = 12 : 4 = 3 : 1 and yellow : green = 3 : 1. The 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio is (3 : 1) × (3 : 1).

Law of independent assortment: when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair. RrYy forms four types of gametes in equal frequency: RY, Ry, rY, ry (each 1/4).
The dihybrid Punnett square has 4 × 4 = 16 boxes. F2 has 9 genotypes. Useful probabilities: RRYY = 1/16; RrYy = 4/16; any homozygous recessive for both (rryy) = 1/16.

example.q: From 1600 F2 seeds of a dihybrid cross RrYy × RrYy, how many are expected to be round green, and how many to be RrYy?

learn.reallife: Plant breeders at ICAR use dihybrid logic to combine two useful traits, like disease resistance and short height, into one wheat variety.

topics.title: Chromosomal theory of inheritance and Morgan's flies

learn.hook: Mendel's work lay ignored for 35 years. In 1900, three scientists independently rediscovered it, and chromosomes soon explained it.
points: Mendel published his work in 1865 but it went unrecognised until 1900, for reasons such as poor communication, his idea of discrete factors that did not blend, and his mathematical approach being new to biology. In 1900 de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak independently rediscovered his results.
By then, better microscopes let scientists watch cell division. Chromosomes, like genes, occur in pairs; the two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes.
Parallel behaviour: chromosomes and genes both occur in pairs; both segregate at gamete formation so only one of each pair reaches a gamete; independent pairs segregate independently of each other.
Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted this parallel. Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles: the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

Thomas Hunt Morgan and colleagues verified it experimentally with the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. Reasons: it can be grown on simple synthetic medium in the lab; it completes its life cycle in about two weeks; a single mating produces many progeny; male and female flies are easily distinguishable; many hereditary variations are visible with low-power microscopes.

example.q: Give four reasons why Drosophila melanogaster suits genetic experiments.
steps: Easily grown on a simple synthetic medium.
Short life cycle of about two weeks.
Large number of progeny from a single mating.
Clear differentiation of sexes and many visible hereditary variations.
example.answer: Simple medium, two-week life cycle, many progeny, easily distinguished sexes and visible variations.

learn.reallife: Indian labs, such as those at the National Centre for Biological Sciences in Bengaluru, still use Drosophila to study genes for development and disease.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How did people link Mendel's factors to chromosomes, and why did Morgan love fruit flies?'
teach.praise: Bravo! Sutton and Boveri saw genes and chromosomes behave alike, and Morgan proved it with quick-breeding fruit flies.
teach.nudge: Good! Who noticed the parallel, and why are fruit flies so handy for experiments?

learn.hook: Morgan's flies broke Mendel's 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 rule, and the reason led to the first gene maps.
points: Morgan carried out dihybrid crosses in Drosophila for sex-linked genes. E.g. yellow-bodied, white-eyed females × brown-bodied, red-eyed (wild type) males, then intercrossing the F1. The F2 ratios deviated significantly from 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, as the two genes did not segregate independently.

When genes are grouped on the same chromosome, some are very tightly linked (very low recombination) and others loosely linked (higher recombination). In Morgan's crosses, yellow body and white eye gave 1.3 per cent recombinants; white eye and miniature wing gave 37.2 per cent.

Linkage (a term coined by Morgan) is the physical association of genes on a chromosome. Recombination is the generation of non-parental gene combinations. Crossing over during meiosis is the physical exchange between homologous chromosomes that produces recombination.
Alfred Sturtevant, Morgan's student, used the frequency of recombination between gene pairs on the same chromosome as a measure of the distance between genes and 'mapped' their positions.

Distinguish: dominance (one allele masks the other), incomplete dominance (intermediate heterozygote), co-dominance (both expressed). Aneuploidy (gain or loss of chromosomes) differs from polyploidy (whole sets increase).

example.q: Genes A and B show 2 per cent recombination; genes B and C show 30 per cent. Which pair is more tightly linked, and which pair is farther apart on the chromosome?
steps: Lower recombination means tighter linkage and shorter distance.
A–B (2%) is tightly linked and close together.
B–C (30%) is loosely linked and farther apart.
example.answer: A and B are tightly linked; B and C are farther apart.

learn.reallife: Modern gene mapping used in breeding rice varieties at IRRI and ICAR still begins with Sturtevant's idea that recombination frequency reflects distance.

learn.hook: Human height comes in thousands of shades between short and tall, not just two boxes. That's polygenic inheritance.
points: Polygenic traits are controlled by three or more genes, and the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele (additive effect). They show continuous variation, like human height and skin colour. Environment also influences them.
Skin colour example with three genes A, B and C: dominant alleles A, B, C add to dark pigment. AABBCC is darkest, aabbcc lightest, and AaBbCc (three dominant alleles) is intermediate.
Pleiotropy: a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions. Usually the gene affects a metabolic pathway that contributes to different phenotypes.

Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an example: an inborn error of metabolism, autosomal recessive. The affected person lacks the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine. Phenylalanine accumulates and is converted into phenylpyruvic acid and other derivatives.

Accumulation in the brain causes mental retardation, and these are also excreted in urine because of poor absorption by the kidney. Affected persons also show reduced hair and skin pigmentation, so one gene gives several effects (pleiotropy).

example.q: In the three-gene model of skin colour, how many dominant alleles do AaBBCc and aaBbcc each carry? Which is darker?
steps: AaBBCc: A (1) + B, B (2) + C (1) = 4 dominant alleles.
aaBbcc: B (1) = 1 dominant allele.
More dominant alleles add more pigment.

learn.reallife: Newborn screening programmes in several Indian states test for PKU so a special low-phenylalanine diet can prevent brain damage.

topics.title: Sex determination: XO, XY and ZW systems

learn.hook: In birds, it is the mother who decides whether a chick is male or female. Biology does not follow one rule for all.
points: In 1891 Henking traced a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis of some insects. Half the sperms received it and half did not. He called it the X body; it was later named the X-chromosome.
Chromosomes involved in sex determination are sex chromosomes; the rest are autosomes.
XO type (e.g. grasshopper): all eggs carry an X; males have only one X besides autosomes (XO), and females have two X (XX).

XY type (e.g. Drosophila, humans): males have an X and a smaller Y (XY), females XX. Both XO and XY are examples of male heterogamety, since males produce two kinds of gametes (with or without X, or with X or Y).
ZW type (e.g. birds): females have one Z and one W (ZW) and males have two Z (ZZ). This is female heterogamety; females produce two kinds of gametes.

example.q: In a bird species, what is the probability that a chick is female, and which parent's gamete decides it?
steps: Females are ZW and produce Z eggs and W eggs in equal numbers.
Males are ZZ and produce only Z sperms.
A W egg + Z sperm gives a ZW female: probability 1/2.
example.answer: 1/2; decided by the mother's egg (female heterogamety).

learn.reallife: Poultry farms in Namakkal sort chicks by sex for egg-laying units; the genetics behind the female deciding chick sex is the ZW system.

topics.title: Sex determination in humans and honey bees

learn.hook: A male honey bee has a grandfather but no father, and it can have grandsons but never sons.
points: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes, the same in both sexes, and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX in females, XY in males).

All eggs carry X. Males produce 50 per cent X-bearing and 50 per cent Y-bearing sperms. An X sperm gives a female (XX), a Y sperm a male (XY). So there is a 50 per cent probability of a male or female child in each pregnancy, and the father's sperm decides the sex. It is wrong to blame women for the sex of a child.
Honey bees show a haplodiploid system. An offspring from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker); an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by parthenogenesis.

Males have half the number of chromosomes of females: females are diploid with 32 chromosomes and males haploid with 16. Males produce sperms by mitosis. Males have no father and so cannot have sons, but they have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

example.q: Using a simple honey bee pedigree, explain why a drone has a grandfather but no father.
steps: A drone develops from an unfertilised egg laid by the queen, so it has a mother but no father.
The queen herself developed from a fertilised egg, so she had a father (a drone).
That drone is the grandfather of our drone.
example.answer: A drone has a mother (queen) but no father; the queen's father is the drone's grandfather.

learn.reallife: Beekeepers in Himachal Pradesh and Punjab know that drones come from unfertilised eggs; managing queen fertility is the key to a strong hive.

learn.hook: A single wrong letter among millions in a gene can bend red blood cells into sickles.
points: Mutation is a phenomenon that results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently changes the genotype and phenotype of an organism. Besides recombination, mutation is a source of variation.
Loss (deletion) or gain (insertion or duplication) of a segment of DNA results in alteration in chromosomes. Such chromosomal aberrations are commonly observed in cancer cells.
A point mutation is a change in a single base pair of DNA, e.g. sickle-cell anaemia. Deletions and insertions of base pairs cause frame-shift mutations.
Mutagens are chemical and physical factors that induce mutations; UV radiation is an example.

Sickle-cell anaemia: autosomal recessive; Glu is replaced by Val at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain due to a single base substitution at the sixth codon (GAG → GUG). The mutant haemoglobin changes RBCs from biconcave discs to elongated sickle shapes under low oxygen tension. HbᴬHbˢ heterozygotes are carriers with sickle-cell trait; disease needs both parents to be carriers or affected.

example.q: Two carriers (HbᴬHbˢ) of sickle-cell trait plan a family. What is the probability that a child will (a) have the disease, (b) be a carrier?
steps: HbᴬHbˢ × HbᴬHbˢ → HbᴬHbᴬ : HbᴬHbˢ : HbˢHbˢ = 1 : 2 : 1.
(a) Diseased (HbˢHbˢ) = 1/4.
(b) Carrier (HbᴬHbˢ) = 2/4 = 1/2.

learn.reallife: India's National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission screens people in tribal regions, offering counselling to carrier couples, because the disease is common in parts of central India.

topics.title: Pedigree analysis, Mendelian disorders and thalassemia

learn.hook: Family trees are not just for weddings. Doctors read them like maps to track a disease across generations.
points: Pedigree analysis is the study of a trait across several generations of a family. Standard symbols: square = male, circle = female, shaded symbol = affected, diamond = sex unspecified, horizontal line between male and female = mating, double line = consanguineous mating, vertical line down = offspring.

Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene. They follow Mendelian inheritance, can be traced by pedigree analysis, and may be dominant or recessive, autosomal or sex-linked. Examples: haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia.

Pedigree clues: autosomal dominant traits (e.g. myotonic dystrophy) appear in every generation and an affected child has at least one affected parent. Autosomal recessive traits (e.g. sickle-cell anaemia) can skip generations; two unaffected carrier parents can have an affected child; males and females are affected equally.

Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive blood disease transmitted when both parents are unaffected carriers. A mutation or deletion reduces the rate of synthesis of one of the globin chains (α or β), forming abnormal haemoglobin and causing anaemia.

α thalassemia: production of α globin is affected; controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 of each parent (four genes in all); the more genes affected, the less α globin. β thalassemia: β globin affected; controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11 of each parent. Thalassemia is a quantitative problem (too few globin molecules), while sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem (incorrectly functioning globin).

example.q: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Is the trait dominant or recessive? Can it be X-linked recessive?
steps: Unaffected parents with an affected child means the trait is recessive; both parents are carriers.
For an X-linked recessive daughter to be affected, her father must be affected.
The father is unaffected, so the trait must be autosomal recessive.
example.answer: Autosomal recessive; it cannot be X-linked recessive since the father is unaffected.

learn.reallife: Many Indian states run thalassemia carrier screening for students and couples, since counselling two carriers can prevent a child's lifelong transfusion needs.

topics.title: Sex-linked disorders: haemophilia and colour blindness

learn.hook: Queen Victoria was a carrier of haemophilia, and the gene spread through royal families of Europe.
points: Haemophilia: a sex-linked recessive disease in which a single protein in the cascade of clotting proteins is affected. A simple cut may lead to non-stop bleeding.

A heterozygous female (carrier) may transmit it to sons. A haemophilic female is extremely rare because her mother must be at least a carrier and her father must be haemophilic. Queen Victoria's family pedigree shows many haemophilic descendants, as she was a carrier.

Colour blindness: a sex-linked recessive disorder due to a defect in either the red or the green cone of the eye, causing failure to discriminate between red and green. The mutation is in certain genes on the X chromosome. It occurs in about 8 per cent of males and only about 0.4 per cent of females.

Cross problems: a carrier mother (XᴴXʰ) × normal father (XᴴY) gives daughters 1/2 normal, 1/2 carrier; sons 1/2 normal, 1/2 affected. A daughter is colour blind only if her mother is at least a carrier and her father is colour blind.

example.q: A carrier woman for haemophilia (XᴴXʰ) marries a normal man (XᴴY). What fraction of all their children will be haemophilic, and which sex will they be?
steps: Mother's eggs: Xᴴ or Xʰ; father's sperms: Xᴴ or Y.
Children: XᴴXᴴ, XᴴY, XʰXᴴ, XʰY, each 1/4.
Only XʰY is haemophilic: 1/4 of all children, all sons.
example.answer: 1/4 of all children; affected children are sons (1/2 of the sons).

learn.reallife: Haemophilia societies in Indian cities run clotting-factor treatment centres; family screening of carrier women uses exactly these Punnett squares.

quiz.mistake: Thinks females cannot inherit X-linked traits

quiz.q: A colour-blind man and a carrier woman have a daughter. What is the probability that she is colour blind?
quiz.explain: Daughter gets the father's Xᶜ (colour-blind allele) for sure, and the mother's Xᶜ with probability 1/2.
steps: Father always gives his X (colour-blind) to daughters
Mother gives the colour-blind X with probability 1/2
quiz.mistake: Forgets the daughter always gets the father's X

quiz.q: Colour blindness is caused by a defect in
options: either the red or the green cone of the eye
quiz.explain: A mutation in X-linked genes affects red or green cones, causing failure to discriminate red from green.
quiz.mistake: Thinks rods or the lens are involved

quiz.q: From the cross XᴴXʰ × XᴴY, what fraction of daughters will be carriers?
quiz.explain: Daughters receive Xᴴ from the father and Xᴴ or Xʰ from the mother, so half are XᴴXʰ carriers.
steps: Daughters: XᴴXᴴ or XᴴXʰ, each 1/2
quiz.mistake: Gives the fraction of all children

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why are haemophilia and colour blindness much more common in boys?'
teach.praise: Perfect! The genes are X-linked recessive; males have only one X, so one faulty copy shows, while females need two.
teach.nudge: Good! Which chromosome carries these genes, and why does that matter for males?

topics.title: Chromosomal disorders: Down's, Klinefelter's and Turner's

learn.hook: One extra copy of the smallest human autosome changes development dramatically. That is Down's syndrome.
points: Chromosomal disorders are caused by absence, excess or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes. Failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division causes gain or loss of a chromosome: aneuploidy. Failure of cytokinesis after telophase increases a whole set of chromosomes: polyploidy, often seen in plants. Trisomy = an additional copy; monosomy = lack of one chromosome of a pair.

Down's syndrome: trisomy of chromosome 21. Features: short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with characteristic palm crease; physical, psychomotor and mental development is retarded. First described by Langdon Down in 1866.

Klinefelter's syndrome: an additional X chromosome, karyotype 47, XXY. Overall masculine development, but feminine development such as breast development (gynaecomastia) is also expressed. Such individuals are sterile.
Turner's syndrome: absence of one X chromosome, karyotype 45, X0. Such females are sterile as ovaries are rudimentary, and they lack other secondary sexual characters.

example.q: Give the chromosome number and sex chromosomes for (a) Down's syndrome male, (b) Klinefelter's syndrome, (c) Turner's syndrome.
steps: (a) Trisomy 21 adds one autosome to 46: 47, with XY in a male.
(b) One extra X: 47, XXY.
(c) One X missing: 45, X0.

learn.reallife: Prenatal screening offered in Indian hospitals can detect trisomy 21 early, helping families prepare with medical and educational support.

quiz.explain: 44 autosomes + XXY = 47.
